newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: PDVSA rejects environment critics in Orinoco delta.
newsitem.headline: PDVSA rejects environment critics in Orinoco delta.

text.p: Venezuela's state oil company on Monday denied that it was causing environmental damage or harming an American Indian tribe in the Orinoco delta, as alleged by environmentalist group Orinoco Oilwatch last week.

The delta area, which is home to 25,000 Warao Indians, has seen an explosion of oil activity since 1993 when Venezuela opened some old oilfields and new exploration blocks to foreign contractors in 1993.

"The oil industry is not going to destroy the environment or the Warao people," said Freddy Muziotti, a spokesman for Corporacion Venezolana de Petroleos (CVP), a subsidiary of state- owned Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA).

"There are a lot of people who are holding up the Warao as a flag to take revenge for old grudges," Muzotti added. "They are trying to represent the Warao, but none of these international organisations can represent the Warao because the Warao have not given them the right to."
Orinoco Oilwatch was particularly critical of British Petroleum for its work in the Pedernales field where it has been working as a contractor for state subsidiary Lagoven.
It called for all exploration and production contracts with foreign companies in the delta to be cancelled and said this was a demand of the Warao.

The group, which also encompasses "national-political interests" said, "the opening up of mineral resources has raised serious questions of violation of the Venezuelan Constitution and laws and its threat to national and fiscal sovereignty."

But CVP's Muziotti denied the Warao wanted the oil companies out. He said the industry went to meet the Indians in the delta town of Tucupita earlier this month and the Warao had asked Orinoco Oilwatch to leave the meeting.

"We spent a day explaining to the Guarao what we are doing in the delta and the Guarao did not ask the companies to leave. They are going to name a committee to deal directly with the oil companies to discuss the problems they see there, but they don't want intermediaries."
He said illnesses, such as gastro-enteriritis, were widespread in Warao communities, and the oil industry wanted to change this.

"The Warao are an indigenous group living in very difficult conditions. The Venezuelan oil industry is responsible for what is going to happen there and its goal is to improve the living conditions of a sick people," Muziotti said.
